paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The exponential distribution is a probability distribution controlled by a single number, λ > 0, usually called the rate parameter. Its values run over the interval [0, ∞), so it never goes below zero. If a random variable X follows it, we write X ~ Exp(λ). It is used to analyse Poisson point processes and turns up in many other settings as well.

paragraphs.heading: A name to keep apart
paragraphs.text: The exponential distribution should not be confused with the exponential families of distributions. That is a large class of probability distributions. The exponential distribution belongs to it, but so do many others, including the normal, binomial, gamma and Poisson distributions.

paragraphs.heading: Average and spread
paragraphs.text: If X has rate λ, its mean, or expected value, is E [X] = 1/λ. Think of someone who gets two phone calls an hour on average: they can expect 0.5 hour, or 30 minutes, between one call and the next. The variance is Var [X] = 1/λ². That makes the standard deviation equal to the mean.

paragraphs.heading: It has no memory
paragraphs.text: Read X as a waiting time for some event. If you have already waited a while and nothing has happened, the time you still have to wait has exactly the same distribution as it did at the very start. For instance, if the event has not happened after 30 seconds, the chance it takes at least 10 more seconds equals the chance, from the start, of it taking more than 10 seconds. Only the exponential and geometric distributions are memoryless in this way. It follows that the exponential is the only continuous probability distribution with a constant failure rate.

paragraphs.heading: Maximum entropy
paragraphs.text: Consider every continuous probability distribution living on [0, ∞) with a given mean μ. Of all of them, the one with the largest differential entropy is the exponential with rate λ = 1/μ. Put another way, if a random quantity is never negative and you fix only its expected value, the exponential is the maximum entropy distribution for it.

paragraphs.heading: Family ties
paragraphs.text: Scaling keeps it in the family: if X ∼ Exp(λ) and c > 0, then cX ∼ Exp(λ/c). Adding two independent exponential variables with the same rate gives an Erlang distribution with shape 2, which is itself a special case of the gamma distribution. More generally, the sum of n independent Exp(λ) variables is Gamma(n, λ) distributed. Turning that around, Exp(λ) is the same as Gamma(1, λ) and Erlang(1, λ).
